title: Which Departments Should Adopt AI First?
summary: A ranked order of departments for an AI rollout, plus criteria to pick the best one: AI-friendly work, adoption gap, turnaround time, readiness and risk.
body_markdown:
**Quick answer:** Start with **customer support** and **marketing and sales** . Most of their work is writing, research and repeat questions. Slow replies and drafts hold up customers and other teams. **Engineering and IT** are often ahead already, so support them. Put **finance, operations and HR** second. Put **legal and compliance** last, and start narrow. To choose for your own company, rank departments by value, then check readiness and risk. Value is the AI-friendly hours people still spend without AI, weighted by how much slow turnaround holds up others.


You cannot roll out AI to every department at once, so the order matters. This guide gives a default order. Gives a criterion for you to decide which rollout order is applicable for your organization. It is written for HR, IT and operations leaders who set the rollout.


The default order is a judgment. It comes from what each department does all week and where slow turnaround holds up other teams. It is not the result of a department-level study. The surveys cited here report AI use by industry and job level, not by department. The criteria section shows how to replace the judgment with your own numbers.


## The default order: which departments should adopt AI first


Order Department Why it goes here Start with


First Customer support Most work is text. Slow replies reach customers. Reply drafts, ticket summaries, help-article search


First Marketing and sales Drafts, research and follow-ups wait on people. First drafts, call summaries, account research


Already ahead Engineering and IT Often using AI weekly already. The gap is smallest. Approved tools and shared practices


Second Finance Reports and the month-end close wait on analysis. The data is sensitive. Data cleanup and variance drafts, with written data rules


Second Operations Requests wait on routine work, if much of it is office work. Summaries, forms and repeat requests


Second HR Questions and drafts fit AI. Hiring uses are high-risk. Policy questions, job descriptions, training material


Last Legal and compliance Contract reviews hold up other teams. The material is privileged. One narrow, approved use


## Criteria for choosing the best department to start with


These criteria fit any size or industry. Every input comes from your own people, tools and numbers.


Turnaround time is how long work takes from arrival to being finished and handed on. A customer waiting for a reply is one example. The finance team closing the month is another. A role group is a set of employees who do the same kind of job in a department. Outbound sales reps, account executives and support agents are examples.


The nine criteria fall into three groups. Value ranks departments. Readiness sets timing. Risk sets how to start.


Group Criterion Exactly what to record Where it comes from


Value 1. AI-friendly hours per person Weekly hours one person in the role group spends on tasks that pass the task test. Example: 14. The department head's list of the group's 10 most frequent tasks


Value 2. Employees in the role group Active employees whose job title is in the role group, counted in full-time equivalents on the scoring day. A half-time employee counts 0.5. Leave out open positions. Count contractors only if they do the same work in the same tools. Example: 60. The HR system's employee list, filtered by job title


Value 3. Share not yet using AI Take the share of the group that used an AI tool on at least one day in a week. Average it over the last 4 full weeks. Enter 100% minus that average. Example: 30% used one weekly, so enter 70%. Usage metadata from your AI tools


Value 4. Importance (1 to 3) The higher of two scores. Turnaround score: 3 if slow turnaround here delays customers, revenue or several teams. 2 if it delays one team or an internal deadline. 1 if it delays nobody. Cost band: 3, 2 or 1 if cost per hour is in the top, middle or bottom third of your departments. Department heads for turnaround. Finance for cost per hour.


Readiness 5. Manager and champion (0 to 2) 2 if the manager used an AI tool in each of the last 4 weeks and a named champion exists. 1 if only one is true. 0 if neither. A champion uses AI on at least 3 days a week and has agreed to coach teammates. Usage metadata for the manager. The department head for the champion.


Readiness 6. Approved tool in the team's daily apps (0 to 2) 2 if an approved AI tool is built into the apps the team uses daily, and every person in the group has a seat. Apps include email, ticketing and documents. 1 if a tool exists but some people lack seats, or it sits outside those apps. 0 if there is none. IT


Readiness 7. A result you can measure (0 to 2) 2 if the team reports a number AI should move at least monthly, with 3 months of history. Examples: tickets resolved per hour, days to close the books. 1 if the number exists but is not tracked regularly. 0 if there is none. The team's own reports


Readiness 8. Next team can keep up (0 to 2) Ask the head of the receiving team: could you handle 20% more per week with no longer wait? 2 for yes. 1 for some, with a queue. 0 for no. The receiving team's head


Risk 9. Risk level (low, medium or high) The higher of two levels: data sensitivity and the cost of a wrong answer. Step 4 defines the levels. Security and legal


### How to apply the criteria in five steps


The table lists what to record. The five steps below show the order of work. Step 1 finds criterion 1. Step 2 uses criteria 1 to 4 to rank departments. Step 3 scores criteria 5 to 8. Step 4 sets criterion 9. Step 5 turns the scores into a decision. The table shows where criteria 2 to 4 come from. The section "Find the numbers in your own data" shows how to pull them.


### Step 1: Find the work AI can speed up


For each role group, ask the department head for the 10 tasks the group repeats most. Ask for the weekly hours one person spends on each. A task is AI-friendly if it passes at least 4 of these 5 tests:


- Text, numbers or code go in, and text, numbers or code come out.
- The team does it at least weekly.
- A person can check the result in a few minutes.
- A wrong first draft costs little, because someone reviews it first.
- The material is in a tool AI can reach: email, documents, tickets, a CRM or a code repository. A CRM is the system where a sales team records its customers.


Add the weekly hours of the tasks that pass. That sum is the group's AI-friendly hours per person.[Task-level usage data](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/how-to-identify-which-tasks-your-employees-are-automating-with-ai) shows which tasks teams already hand to AI.


Illustrative example, not customer data. Share of AI use by type of task, for six departments. It shows which departments' work is mostly writing, research, data or code.


### Step 2: Rank departments by value


Value = AI-friendly hours per person × employees in the role group × share not yet using AI × importance. Use criteria 1 to 4. Work it out for each role group. Add the results for the department.


An hour saved is worth more where customers or other teams are waiting. Look for waits caused by drafting, summarizing or looking things up. AI shortens those waits. A faster draft does not shorten a wait for sign-off.


### Step 3: Check readiness


Score criteria 5 to 8 with the 0, 1 or 2 rules in the table. The total is 0 to 8.


[Gallup's May 2026 tracking](https://www.gallup.com/699797/indicator-artificial-intelligence.aspx) calls manager support the strongest driver of widespread adoption. In organizations that have adopted AI, some employees strongly agree their manager actively supports AI use. They are 1.7 times as likely to use it a few times a week or more. Only 36% of employees in those organizations strongly agree their manager does. If the manager is not on board, fix that first. For training, see[role-based AI training](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/ai-employee-training-the-fast-track-blueprint-for-company-wide-ai-adoption) .


Criterion 8 matters because time can just move. Suppose a team writes drafts twice as fast, but approvers still review one a day. The team gains nothing.


### Step 4: Check risk


Take the higher of the data level and the wrong-answer level.


- Low: internal, non-sensitive text. Review catches a wrong answer before it reaches anyone. Use approved tools openly.
- Medium: customer or financial data, or a wrong answer that could reach a customer or distort a report. Use approved tools. Write down what data can go in.
- High: regulated or privileged material, hiring decisions, or a wrong answer that could harm a customer or break a law. Start with one narrow use. A person reviews every output.[The EU AI Act lists](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3/) AI that filters job applications or evaluates candidates as high-risk.


Skipping a department does not remove the risk. People may use unapproved tools on their own. That is[shadow AI](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/what-is-shadow-ai) .


### Step 5: Decide, and break ties


- Start now: readiness of 5 or more, and low or medium risk.
- Prepare first: readiness under 5. Name the missing item (manager, champion, approved tool, measure or next team) and fix it first.
- Start narrow: high risk, whatever the score.


If two departments tie, pick the one with more newer or less experienced staff.[The customer support study described below](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.11771) found the biggest gains there. The scores and cutoffs are rules of thumb, not research findings. Adjust them when you see your own spread.


### Example with four made-up departments


The numbers are invented to show the arithmetic. They are not data from any company.


Department Employees AI-friendly hours each Not yet using AI Importance Value Readiness (of 8) Decision


Customer support 60 14 70% 3 1,764 6 Start now, with written data rules


Marketing 25 16 50% 2 400 7 Start now


Finance 25 8 60% 3 360 5 Start now, with written data rules


Operations 200 2 80% 1 320 3 Prepare first


Operations has more than three times the employees of customer support, yet it ranks last. Little of its work is AI-friendly. Almost nothing waits on it. Its readiness is 3 of 8, so it prepares first.


## Department by department: what to start with


### Customer support: first


- AI-friendly tasks: drafting replies, summarizing long ticket threads, finding the right help article.
- Where turnaround is slow: time to first reply and time to resolve. Customers wait on every ticket.
- A person still checks: the reply before sending, and any refund or account change.
- Number to watch: tickets resolved per hour, and time to first reply.
- Evidence: a study of 5,172 customer support agents at one Fortune 500 software company used data from 2020 and 2021. An AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 15% on average. Less experienced and lower-skilled workers improved in speed and quality. The most experienced saw small gains in speed and small declines in quality. Expect less from a team of veterans.


### Marketing and sales: first


- AI-friendly tasks: first drafts of emails, campaign copy and proposals; call and meeting summaries; account research.
- Where turnaround is slow: campaigns wait for a first draft. Proposals wait to be written. Follow-ups wait after a call.
- A person still checks: claims, prices, customer names and anything promised.
- Number to watch: time from a call to the follow-up email, and time to a first proposal draft.


Score by role group: outbound reps, account executives and field reps spend very different time on these tasks.


### Engineering and IT: usually already ahead


- AI-friendly tasks: code suggestions, writing tests, summarizing incidents and tickets, answering help desk questions.
- Where turnaround is slow: waiting for a code review, and waiting for help desk answers.
- A person still checks: code review before anything ships.
- Number to watch: time for a code change to be reviewed, and help desk time to first reply.
- Why already ahead: in the same Gallup tracking, daily AI use was 42% in the technology industry. It was 27% in finance, 22% in professional services and 9% to 15% in the other seven industries. Gallup measures industries, not departments, so treat this as a hint. If your engineers already use AI weekly, the gap is small. Support them with approved tools. Ask their heaviest users to act as champions for other teams.


### Finance, operations and HR: second


Finance. Tasks: summarizing contracts and invoices, drafting variance explanations, cleaning data exports, answering policy questions. Turnaround: days to close the books, which every team waits on. A person checks every number against its source. Risk is medium, so use approved tools and written data rules.


Operations. Tasks: summarizing requests, drafting standard procedures, filling forms, answering repeat internal questions. Turnaround: days a request waits before someone acts. Operations varies between companies, so run the task test before ranking it.


HR. Tasks: policy questions, job descriptions, training material, survey-comment summaries. Turnaround: time to answer an employee question, and time to a first job description draft. Keep candidate screening out of early pilots. It is high-risk.


### Legal and compliance, and work away from a desk: last


Legal and compliance handle privileged and confidential material. Mistakes cost the most. Contracts waiting for review can hold up sales and finance, so the turnaround score is high. Risk sets the pace anyway. Start with one narrow, approved use, such as summarizing internal documents. A person reviews every output.


Work away from a desk comes last, as a separate project. Run the task test on each role. Little of the week is spent in tools AI can reach, so AI-friendly hours will be low.


## Find the numbers in your own data


Four inputs come from your own people. HR gives headcount. Each manager gives a task list. Finance gives cost per hour. Each department head gives the turnaround answer. The adoption gap and the depth of use come from usage metadata. That is a record of which AI tool was used on which days, grouped by team. It holds no prompt or output content.


List the role groups. Take the departments from HR. Split each into role groups. In sales, score outbound reps, account executives and field reps separately.


Pull weekly use for each group. Weekly use is the share of people who used an AI tool on at least one day in a week. Average it over the last 4 full weeks. Collect it from every AI tool you pay for. Departments often use different tools: a team on ChatGPT shows nothing in a Copilot report. See[one view across Claude, Copilot and Gemini](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/unified-ai-tool-dashboard) . Compare groups on the same[AI adoption metrics](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/tracking-employee-ai-adoption-which-metrics-matter) .


Worklytics sample report, illustrative, not customer data. Share of employees who used each AI tool at least once in the past month, by department. Departments lean on different tools.


Find the gap. Subtract weekly use from 100%. That is the share not yet using AI. A group far below your top group has a big gap.


Worklytics sample report, illustrative, not customer data. How AI use is spread inside each department, from not using AI to using it four or more days a week.


Read the depth of use. Count the days a week people use AI. Note how much they do on those days. Many people using AI once a week for one task is a different problem from fewer people using it daily for many tasks. The[AI maturity curve](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/the-ai-maturity-curve-measuring-ai-adoption-in-your-organization) moves from adoption to proficiency to productivity gains.


Worklytics sample report, illustrative, not customer data. Departments placed by days a week of AI use and how much they do on those days.


Score and re-score. Enter the numbers in the criteria table. Run them again after each round, because gaps move.


### Where a usage tool fits, and what it cannot show


Worklytics is one tool that can cover pulling weekly use, finding the gap and reading the depth of use. It reads usage metadata from tools such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Slack. It reports that data by[team and role](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/ai-usage-checker-track-ai-usage-by-team-role) . Its usage view shows:


- Active users: people who used a tool, not only people who hold a license.
- Usage by tool.
- How often people use AI.
- How many different uses each team has.
- Coverage gaps: teams that have access but little real use.


It reports at group level from anonymized, aggregated data. No one person's activity is shown. It can also compare your rates with similar companies.


What it does not show. It reads metadata only. It cannot show what the work contained or whether the output was good. It sees only the tools connected to it. Judge turnaround against numbers each department already tracks, such as time to first reply or days to close the books.


## What this order cannot tell you


The default order is judgment. It comes from the makeup of each department's work. One field study backs customer support. The rest rests on reasoning about tasks, turnaround and risk.


Departments are not uniform. A sales department holds outbound reps and account executives whose work differs. Split large departments by role before you compare them.


Usage is not value. A department can use AI daily and still wait just as long for work to move on. Judge a pilot on the turnaround number you chose, not on logins.


Small teams are noisy. Two people starting or stopping use moves a five-person team by 40 points.


## Frequently asked questions


### Which department should adopt AI first?


Customer support and marketing and sales are the usual first picks. Most of their work is writing, research and repeat questions. Slow replies and drafts hold up customers and other teams. Engineering and IT are often ahead already. Finance, operations and HR come second. Legal and compliance come last. Confirm the order with the criteria in this guide.


### How do you choose the best department to start AI adoption?


Rank departments by value: AI-friendly hours per person, times employees in the role group, times the share not yet using AI, times importance. Then score readiness from 0 to 8 and set the risk level. Start now where readiness is 5 or more and risk is low or medium.


### Should the department with the most people go first?


Not by headcount alone. Headcount matters only if the work is AI-friendly and people are not already using AI. In this guide's made-up example, operations has more than three times the employees of customer support. It still ranks last. Little of its work is AI-friendly, and it is not ready.


### Which tasks are easiest for AI?


Tasks that pass at least 4 of 5 tests. Text, numbers or code go in and come out. The team repeats the task weekly. A person can check the result in a few minutes. A wrong first draft costs little. The material sits in a tool AI can reach. Examples: drafting replies, summarizing tickets or calls, first drafts of emails and proposals, and answering repeat internal questions.


### Should engineering adopt AI first?


Engineering and IT are often ahead already. Gallup finds daily AI use of 42% in the technology industry as of May 2026. Gallup measures industries, not departments. If your engineers already use AI weekly, support them with approved tools. Ask their heaviest users to coach other teams.


### Is HR a good first department for AI?


Not first. Policy questions, job descriptions and training material fit AI. Hiring uses are high-risk. The EU AI Act lists AI that filters job applications or evaluates candidates as high-risk. Start HR in the second group, with uses that do not involve hiring decisions.


### How do you measure AI adoption by department?


Use usage metadata: which AI tool was used on which days, grouped by department, with no prompt or output content. Weekly use is the share of people who used an AI tool on at least one day in a week. Average it over the last 4 full weeks. Combine every tool the company pays for. Then departments on different tools can be compared.


To see these numbers for your own departments,[Worklytics' AI adoption page](https://www.worklytics.co/ai-adoption) shows what it reports by team and role. You can also request a demo there. It shows how much AI is used and where. Whether the work improved still takes your managers' input.
